'''Tie''': {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Rick Santorum]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Rick Santorum]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsPA}} {{Rick Santorum series}} The '''2000 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania''' was held on November 7, 2000. Republican incumbent [[Rick Santorum]] was re-elected to a second term in office over Democratic congressman [[Ron Klink]].{{Cite web |url=http://www.electionreturns.state.pa.us/ElectionsInformation.aspx?FunctionID=13&ElectionID=2&OfficeID=2 |title=Commonwealth of PA - Elections Information |access-date=2008-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080515031139/http://www.electionreturns.state.pa.us/ElectionsInformation.aspx?FunctionID=13&ElectionID=2&OfficeID=2 |archive-date=2008-05-15 |url-status=dead }} [[Pennsylvania]] was considered a [[swing state]] in the concurrent [[United States presidential election]].Resnick, Jolyn and Kalen Churcher. "[https://www.newspapers.com/image/426578774/?terms=Santorum&match=1 Supporters rally in area for candidates]." Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania: ''The Times Leader'', November 7, 2000, p. 4 (subscription required).Miller, Rhonda. "[https://www.newspapers.com/image/89877538/?terms=Santorum&match=1 State GOP leaders rally the faithful: Six-city campaign tour ends at county airport]." Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania: ''Pittsburgh Post-Gazette'', November 7, 2000, p. 8 (subscription required). It was ultimately one of four states that elected Republican senators despite being voting for Democratic presidential nominee [[Al Gore]], along with the [[New England]] states of [[2000 United States Senate election in Maine|Maine]], [[2000 United States Senate election in Rhode Island|Rhode Island]] and [[2000 United States Senate election in Vermont|Vermont]]. Republicans would not win the Class 1 Senate seat from Pennsylvania again until [[2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania|2024]]. ==Republican primary== {{Election box begin no change|title=2000 Republican U.S. Senate primary{{cite web|url=https://www.electionreturns.pa.gov/Home/SummaryResults?ElectionID=9&ElectionType=P&IsActive=0|title=Pennsylvania Elections {{!}} Summary Results|access-date=27 Sep 2023}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Rick Santorum]] (inc.) | party = Republican Party (US) | votes = 545,687 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 545,687 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *Phil Berg *[[Tom Foley (Pennsylvania politician)|Tom Foley]], former Pennsylvania labor secretary and [[1994 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|1994 lieutenant governor nominee]] *[[Ron Klink]], U.S. representative from [[Murrysville, Pennsylvania|Murrysville]] *Murray Levin *[[Robert A. Rovner]], former Republican state senator from [[Philadelphia]] *[[Allyson Schwartz]], state senator from [[Northeast Philadelphia]] ===Campaign=== Klink portrayed himself as the only candidate who could defeat Santorum.{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}} ===Results=== [[File:2000 Pennsylvania US Senate Democratic primary by county.svg|thumb|center|250px|Results by county {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#7996E2|Klink}}|{{legend|#BDD3FF|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#A5B0FF|40%–50%}}|{{legend|#7996E2|50%–60%}}|{{legend|#6674DE|60%–70%}}|{{legend|#584CDE|70%–80%}}|{{legend|#3933E5|80%–90%}} }} {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#51C2C2|Schwartz}}|{{legend|#ACF2F2|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#7DDDDD|40%–50%}}|{{legend|#51C2C2|50%–60%}} }} {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#FFB380|Foley}}|{{legend|#FEE5D5|30%–40%}}|{{legend|#FFCCAA|40%–50%}}|{{legend|#FFB380|50%–60%}}|{{legend|#FF9955|60%–70%}} }} ]] {{Election box begin no change|title=2000 Democratic U.S. Senate primary}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Ron Klink]] | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 299,219 | percentage = 40.73 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Allyson Schwartz]] | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 194,763 | percentage = 26.52 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Tom Foley (Pennsylvania politician)|Tom Foley]] | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 184,003 | percentage = 25.05 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Robert A. Rovner|Bob Rovner]] | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 28,031 | percentage = 3.82 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Murray Levin | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 18,903 | percentage = 2.57 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Phil Berg | party = Democratic Party (US) | votes = 9,636 | percentage = 1.31 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 734,575 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Candidates=== *Robert Domske (Reform) *John Featherman (Libertarian) *[[Ron Klink]], U.S. representative from [[Murrysville, Pennsylvania|Murrysville]] (Democratic) *[[Rick Santorum]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1995 (Republican) *Lester Searer (Constitution) ===Campaign=== Santorum had gained a reputation as a polarizing figure during his first term in the Senate, and had lost the support of more moderate members of his own party by 1999,Jesdanun, Anick. "[https://www.newspapers.com/image/552839676/?terms=Santorum%20and%20gay&match=1 Santorum's views not right on]." Danville, Pennsylvania: ''The Danville News'', January 26, 1999, p. 5 (subscription required).Brown, Jack. "[https://www.newspapers.com/image/179240296/?terms=Santorum%20and%20gay&match=1 Former congressman mulls run for Senate]." Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: ''The Philadelphia Inquirer'', January 7, 1999, p. 11 (subscription required). but entered the race with a large fundraising advantage and high levels of support from the political right. Klink was viewed as a viable choice because he was a traditional Democrat on most issues and had strong union ties but also was opposed to abortion rights, which Democrats hoped would return votes to their party in the heavily [[Catholic]] but economically liberal coal regions of the state. The campaign turned increasingly negative as both candidates publicly questioned each other's integrity.Marx, Claude R. "[https://www.newspapers.com/image/503447471/?terms=Santorum&match=1 Santorum, Klink spend final day making pleas for votes: The two candidates for Pennsylvania's U.S. Senate seat both predict victory in hotly contested race]." Hazleton, Pennsylvania: ''Standard-Speaker'', November 7, 2000, p. 1 (subscription required). Enthusiasm around Klink's campaign then waned as liberal Democrats balked at donating to a candidate who was almost as socially conservative as Santorum. This was especially true in Philadelphia, where Klink was all but unknown. Klink was also badly outspent, leaving him unable to expand his presence in the state; he did not run a single advertisement on Philadelphia television stations. Ultimately, Klink only carried eight counties as Santorum, who had achieved nationwide prominence for taking positions against abortion and [[LGBT rights in the United States]], was ultimately able to secure victory.[https://books.google.com/books?id=1J_9q-lIWRkC&q=santorum&pg=PA112 Pennsylvania Elections: Statewide Contests from 1950-2004] ===Debates=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |+ 2000 Pennsylvania U.S. Senate election debate |- ! scope="col" | {{abbr|No.|Number}} ! scope="col" | Date ! scope="col" | Host ! scope="col" | Moderators ! scope="col" | Link ! scope="col" | [[Republican Party (US)|Republican]] ! scope="col" | [[Democratic Party (US)|Democratic]] ! scope="col" | [[Libertarian Party (US)|Libertarian]] ! scope="col" | [[Constitution Party (US)|Constitution]] ! scope="col" | [[Reform Party (US)|Reform]] |- ! colspan="5" rowspan="2" |Key:
